It also seems like the content on the sshole page was written by a person. oh did i say "i"? sorry. i had agent swarms. a lot of them. let's not get into it Like many of us who value the human side of the web, I am looking for ways to keep slop at bay. It seems like LLM detection technology works reasonably well nowadays, with Pangram as the main provider. It is expensive, though! Assuming pangram scans are trustworthy, and it seems they are, we could create a centralized index of pangram scans of articles. I have already set up a prototype where I publish results of my own pangram scans. I could create more users, each tied to its own API key, so others can contribute with scans as well. This is way more resource efficient than everyone running their own scans. What do you think? Assuming pangram scans are trustworthy, and it seems they are not to be overly combative, but i’d love to see some methodology establishing this. my understanding is that they are better than a coin toss, but still very prone to false positives, eg on pre-LLM material. They have a technical report with methodology. There are false positives, but they are extremely rare[^1]. Even if you don't trust their marketing materials, they get tagged often enough that we'd see more examples if false positives were common. (There are some! But it's like a single digit number of examples out of many tens or hundreds of thousands of runs.) I'm guessing your understanding comes from an impression "AI detection services" in general, rather than Pangram in particular. [^1]: as long as you consider "used AI to tweak wording" as a true positive, which they don't distinguish from "entirely written by AI" Requiring my writing to be stylistically approved by a machine is even more gross than having a machine do my writing. I might find this acceptable if bad machine writing was a serious problem and if authors got a “false positive” button to override the machine. Please don’t use Pangram and similar tools to judge the content. It’s a mess and flags even genuine hand-written articles as “AI” (written using pen and paper, and then digitalised). I no longer write and publish long form text because of shit like that. I get that it's coming from a place of good intent and care, but I don't like this idea one bit. The negative repercussions of witch-hunting people[0] with fallible tools would, in my opinion, severely outweigh any positive impact it might have. While we might be able to filter out some slop articles quicker, in return we'd pay dearly for any false positive and negatives. If you're an author who strongly objects to LLMs and would never use one for your posts, yet the machine thinks your article is generated, that brands on you a mark of shame you really don't deserve. If you're an author, who uses LLMs and it somehow flies under the radar, that means your readers have a false impression of what they are reading. Not to mention, the community would actually need to pay in cash too for all this as well... I think the current flagging works fine (even if, at least to me it seems, people occasionally apply them a little overzealously, but that's a different topic). [0]: I know that's not your goal, but if it walks like a duck and talks like a duck... While Claudish and LLM prose is annoying and frustrating to read to me as much as the next person, I don’t think this creates an environment that people would want to participate in. I’d be interested to see some statistics and trends of submissions over time. Would be interesting to see any correlations with the addition and removal of the vibecoding tag or various landmark model releases, provided it’s not used as a shaming device. Vote for what you like that is of a quality you appreciate. Flag where appropriate. I don't like reading slop either, but I agree that this doesn't feel like the right response. If you want to crowdsource something, why not crowdsource a list of sites that promise to not use LLMs in their writing (and make an extension that gives them a like green dot or something on readers like HN/Lobsters)? You can bootstrap by using a regex like "made/written.*hand/on my own/without (AI/LLM)" on articles. I feel like rather than conducting witch hunts we should instead give recognition to the people who produce writing we like. I am not automatically bothered if an LLM was part of the writing process of a document I am reading. I understand that some people are, but, to me, the really upsetting thing is the flood of low-effort, uninteresting spam that we have had to endure since people started using LLMs to write. Putting a number on the amount of LLM use on an article does not resolve this issue. I am not exactly sure why there are so many LLM spam articles. Personally, I do involve LLMs in my writing process, albeit only sparsely to correct grammar, say, or to help me phrase a section I am struggling with. When I write something it's because I want to communicate my thoughts or my work, so, fundamentally, I do not understand why people publish slop articles. This makes me think that the slop articles we are all bothered by are just written in bad faith; to gain visibility, out of vanity, or as an advertisement. This has existed before AI, too, but I guess it wasn't such a problem because people actually had to spend time to write. To me, the problem is the bad faith part, not the LLM part. Checking the amount of LLM use is a bad proxy for detecting bad faith. I really don't know how to deal with this situation, though. To be honest, there existed plenty of articles in the era before LLMs whose style of writing and presentation I found insufferable. Take for instance the recent sshole page ( https://sshhole.com/ ). All of it reads like this: so musl (the libc under alpine) goes ok fine, crypt() just won't return NULL anymore. if it fails, it returns a single character instead. that character can never match a real password, so programs don't crash, they just see a wrong password now guess which character they picked for that "*" yep. the star. again. This style of writing was a thing long before LLMs. It also seems like the content on the sshole page was written by a person. Still, I would appreciate it if things like this were not on here. I am bringing up this example, because this style of writing makes me feel disrespected, just like LLM slop articles do. I would like to see a taste filter or a care filter, but I have no idea how to implement such a thing. Link aggregators like Hacker News and Lobste.rs served this purpose for me in the past, but it's not working as well anymore. Maybe the reason is not actually that people can now use LLMs to write, but, rather, that people have discovered these link aggregators as a great way to boost their profile in an incredibly competitive job market. Or something along those lines. It also seems like the content on the sshole page was written by a person. I'm curious why you think that, as the whole thing gave off extremely claude vibes to me (the diagrams definitely so). The author even says they used agents heavily in their work: oh did i say "i"? sorry. i had agent swarms. a lot of them. let's not get into it So perhaps it is LLM content that you're bouncing off of. I genuinely find their textual output impossible to read, and that's not just because I don't like LLMs for ethical/moral/whatever reasons; something about the way they 'write' just bounces straight off my brain and I have to try really hard for any information to go in. Very well put. I feel exactly the same way about basically everything you wrote! Personally, I can't wait for the "skipping capital letters" fad to blow over. Is there an OSS effort to replicate Pangram? The biggest concern I have with LLM scanners is that they penalized any use of LLMs in the past. This includes people who feel like they need them to improve their writing, or who use them to translate their writing (I understand both of these motivations even though I personally make different decisions). Have these issues been solved? Yes, these issues are solved by the author using their own voice. You can ask an LLM for feedback on your writing, or for the translation for a word, but not directly copy paste sentences it generates. An LLM scanner detecting LLM output is a feature, not a bug. I think both of those use cases are totally suitable for getting a LLM-written flag in lobste.rs - in my experience, mostly on English Wikipedia, they completely compromise the written material (which is unfortunate for translation). I don't know that an automated tool is the best way to go forward, regardless. Nope nope nope. I write all my articles by hand and pangram regularly flags them as LLM-written. I don't know where this "false positives are rare" nonsense is coming from but these tools DO NOT WORK. Look, I don't want to read AI slop as much as the next guy but (as I've said many times) making me who don't use AI defend their innocence is not the way.
